claim: Genetically identical cells in cell culture often exhibit heterogeneous behavior, with only 'lineage primed' cells responding to differentiation inducing signals.
source: In cell culture, genetically identical cells often exhibit heterogeneous behavior, with only 'lineage primed' cells responding to differentiation inducing signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on heterogeneous cell behavior in culture.

claim: Heterogeneity exists during normal embryonic development to allow position independent patterning based on 'salt and pepper' differentiation and sorting out.
source: It has recently been proposed that such heterogeneity exists during normal embryonic development to allow position independent patterning based on 'salt and pepper' differentiation and sorting out.
evidence: This is a proposal cited from recent literature about developmental patterning mechanisms.

claim: The Ras-GTPase regulator gefE is required for normal lineage priming and salt and pepper differentiation.
source: These studies reveal that the Ras-GTPase regulator gefE is required for normal lineage priming and salt and pepper differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic studies described in the manuscript.

claim: Ras-GTPase activity sets the intrinsic response threshold to lineage specific differentiation signals.
source: This is because Ras-GTPase activity sets the intrinsic response threshold to lineage specific differentiation signals.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from experimental data on gefE and RasD function.

claim: gefE expression is uniform during growth.
source: we show that although gefE expression is uniform, transcription of its target, rasD, is both heterogeneous and dynamic
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter gene expression data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: rasD transcription is both heterogeneous and dynamic.
source: we show that although gefE expression is uniform, transcription of its target, rasD, is both heterogeneous and dynamic
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter gene expression and FACS analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cells grown without glucose preferentially become stalk cells when mixed in chimeric development with glucose grown cells.
source: Firstly, cells grown without glucose preferentially become stalk cells when mixed in chimeric development with glucose grown cells (Leach et al., 1973; Noce and Takeuchi, 1985; Blaschke et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by data in Figure 1.

claim: G− cells produce significantly fewer spores than G+ cells when developed together in chimera.
source: Consistent with these observations, we find that cells grown in the absence of glucose (G−) produce significantly fewer spores than cells grown in the presence of glucose (G+) when developed together in chimera (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative spore counting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: G− cells are biased towards the DIF dependent pstO and pstB lineages.
source: our analysis of the patterning of cell types at the slug and fruiting body stages reveals that this is because G− cells are biased towards the DIF dependent pstO and pstB lineages (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of cell type markers in chimeric slugs shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: G− cells are more sensitive to DIF than G+ grown cells.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing G− cells are more sensitive to DIF than G+ grown cells (Thompson and Kay, 2000a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 4A.

claim: The REMI mutant library initially contained approximately 1000 individual blasticidin resistant clones.
source: a REMI mutant library estimated to initially contain approximately 1000 individual blasticidin resistant clones was hatched from a frozen stock two times.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup for the genetic screen.

claim: Inverse PCR revealed the pool of cells in later rounds to be largely composed of clones in which the REMI plasmid had integrated into a small 5′ 42 bp exon within the gefE gene.
source: Inverse PCR revealed the pool of cells in later rounds of each pool selection to be largely composed of clones in which the REMI plasmid had integrated into a small 5′ 42 bp exon within the gefE gene (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by iPCR data and shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: There is no difference in the rate of growth of gefE− mutant cells in either G+ or G− medium compared to wild type.
source: Reconstruction experiments revealed no difference in the rate of growth of gefE− mutant cells in either G+ or G− medium
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: gefE− mutant spores hatch at a faster rate than wild type spores.
source: although gefE− mutant spores did, however, hatch at a faster rate than wild type spores
evidence: This is demonstrated by spore hatching assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: When wild type or gefE− mutant G− grown cells were developed in chimera with G+ wild type cells, mutant G− cells were significantly overrepresented in the spore population of chimeric fruiting bodies.
source: Most importantly, when wild type or gefE− mutant G− grown cells were developed in chimera with G+ wild type cells, mutant G− cells were significantly overrepresented in the spore population of chimeric fruiting bodies (Figure 1E, p<0.04)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative spore counting data shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance.

claim: Mutant G− cells do not show the strong overrepresentation in the collar and back populations of chimeric slugs seen when wild type G− cells are mixed with wild type G+ grown cells.
source: This is because mutant G− cells do not show the strong overrepresentation in the collar and back populations of chimeric slugs seen when wild type G− cells are mixed with wild type G+ grown cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of chimeric slugs shown in Figure 1F.

claim: gefE− cells form more spores than wild type cells when both are grown under identical growth conditions in the presence of glucose.
source: To test this, wild type and mutant cells were grown under identical growth conditions in the presence of glucose before mixing for chimeric development. Under these conditions, gefE− cells still formed more spores than wild type cells (Figure 2A, p<0.01).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative spore counting data shown in Figure 2A with statistical significance.

claim: In chimeric slugs, labelled gefE− mutant cells were enriched in the prespore region and excluded from the DIF dependent pstB and pstO cell fates.
source: In chimeric slugs, labelled mutant cells were enriched in the prespore region and excluded from the DIF dependent pstB and pstO cell fates, whilst labelled wild type cells were localized in the pstB and pstO regions of the slug (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of chimeric slugs shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When GefE expression was driven by a strong constitutive promoter in wild type cells, cells expressing high gefE levels were found largely in the pstO and pstB regions of slugs and in the lower cup of fruiting bodies when mixed with wild type cells.
source: Finally, when GefE expression was driven by a strong constitutive promoter in wild type cells, cells expressing high gefE levels were found largely in the pstO and pstB regions of slugs and in the lower cup of fruiting bodies when mixed with wild type cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of chimeric development shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of gefE is required for biasing cells to adopt DIF dependent pstO and pstB cell fates.
source: Together, these data suggest that expression of gefE is required for biasing cells to adopt DIF dependent pstO and pstB cell fates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimeric development experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Clonal development of gefE− mutant was morphologically identical to that of the wild type.
source: Clonal development was found to be morphologically identical to that of the wild type.
evidence: This is an observation from clonal development experiments.

claim: The number of prespore cells in gefE− mutant slugs was the same as that observed in wild type slugs.
source: Furthermore, the number of prespore cells in gefE− mutant slugs was found to be the same as that observed in wild type slugs
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The total number of spores produced in terminal fruiting bodies was the same for the gefE− mutant as for the wild type.
source: and the total number of spores produced in terminal fruiting bodies was the same for the gefE− mutant as for the wild type (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was no defect in prestalk cell specific gene expression in gefE− mutant slugs or fruiting bodies.
source: There was also no defect in prestalk cell specific gene expression in slugs or fruiting bodies (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of marker gene expression shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The only difference between the clonal development of the gefE− cells and the wild type was a slight, although reproducible, delay in the initiation of aggregation.
source: The only difference between the clonal development of the gefE− cells and the wild type was a slight, although reproducible, delay in the initiation of aggregation (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from clonal development experiments.

claim: The gefE gene is involved in lineage priming rather than lineage commitment.
source: These results are, therefore, consistent with the gefE gene being involved in lineage priming rather than lineage commitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that clonal development is normal but chimeric development shows biases.

claim: The lineage bias of the gefE− mutant cells is dependent on the growth history of the partner genotype.
source: Consistent with this idea, the lineage bias of the gefE− mutant cells was found to be dependent on the growth history of the partner genotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by chimeric development experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: gefE− mutant cells were strongly biased towards DIF dependent fates when grown in the G− medium and then mixed with mutant cells grown in G+ medium.
source: For example, gefE− mutant cells were strongly biased towards DIF dependent fates when grown in the G− medium and then mixed with mutant cells grown in G+ medium (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of chimeric slugs shown in Figure 3C.

claim: gefE− cells are totipotent.
source: These experiments provide strong evidence that gefE− cells are totipotent
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that gefE− cells can form all cell types depending on context.

claim: GefE regulates context dependent/relative DIF dependent lineage bias rather than cell fate choice.
source: and that GefE regulates context dependent/relative DIF dependent lineage bias rather than cell fate choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the totality of chimeric and clonal development experiments.

claim: gefE− mutant cells make fewer stalk cells than wild type across a 1000-fold range of DIF concentrations in the cAMP removal monolayer assay.
source: We found that gefE− mutant cells make fewer stalk cells than wild type across a 1000-fold range of DIF concentrations in the cAMP removal monolayer assay but exhibit similar sensitivity to changes in DIF concentration (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by stalk cell differentiation assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: gefE− mutant cells exhibit similar sensitivity to changes in DIF concentration as wild type cells.
source: We found that gefE− mutant cells make fewer stalk cells than wild type across a 1000-fold range of DIF concentrations in the cAMP removal monolayer assay but exhibit similar sensitivity to changes in DIF concentration (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the parallel dose-response curves in Figure 4A.

claim: Growth in the absence of glucose results in a similar increase in DIF sensitivity in both wild type and gefE− mutant cells.
source: Importantly, growth in the absence of glucose results in a similar increase in DIF sensitivity in both wild type and mutant cells (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing G+ and G− conditions in Figure 4A.

claim: GefE is only required to set basal levels of DIF sensitivity.
source: thus suggesting that GefE is only required to set basal levels of DIF sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that gefE mutation shifts the dose-response curve but doesn't change its shape.

claim: DIF induced gene expression of ecmAO:lacZ and ecmB:lacZ reporters was reduced in the gefE− mutant compared to wild type at all DIF concentrations.
source: In the first experiment, cells were transformed with ecmAO:lacZ or ecmB:lacZ reporter genes. DIF induced gene expression of these reporters was reduced in the gefE− mutant compared to wild type at all DIF concentrations, but showed a similar sensitivity to changes in DIF concentration (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter gene expression assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Endogenous ecmA and ecmB transcript levels in response to DIF induction showed similar patterns in gefE− mutant as reporter genes.
source: A similar result was seen when endogenous ecmA and ecmB transcripts were measured in response to DIF induction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GATAc is a transcription factor that translocates to the nucleus minutes after DIF stimulation.
source: GATAc is a transcription factor that translocates to the nucleus minutes after DIF stimulation and is specifically required for DIF dependent pstB cell differentiation (Keller and Thompson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In gefE− mutant cells basal levels of nuclear GATAc were similar to wild type.
source: In gefE− mutant cells basal levels of nuclear GATAc were similar to wild type.
evidence: This is an observation from GATAc-GFP localization experiments.

claim: When gefE− mutant cells were stimulated with DIF, the rate and duration of GATAc-GFP nuclear accumulation were largely unaffected.
source: Furthermore, when gefE− mutant cells were stimulated with DIF, the rate and duration of GATAc-GFP nuclear accumulation were largely unaffected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Large differences were seen in the number of gefE− mutant cells that exhibit nuclear GATAc accumulation compared to wild type.
source: However, large differences were seen in the number of gefE− mutant cells that exhibit nuclear GATAc accumulation compared to wild type (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of responding cells shown in Figure 4D.

claim: gefE− cells are less sensitive to DIF than wild type cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that gefE− cells are less sensitive to DIF than wild type cells
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple DIF response assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: GefE biases cells towards DIF sensitive fates.
source: consistent with the idea that GefE biases cells towards DIF sensitive fates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the totality of DIF sensitivity experiments.

claim: DIF induced transcription of the prestalk gene, ecmA only occurs once a cell intrinsic threshold is exceeded.
source: It has recently been shown that DIF induced transcription of the prestalk gene, ecmA only occurs once a cell intrinsic threshold is exceeded; increased DIF dose only results in a small change in target gene expression level in each cell, but a much larger increase in the number of cells that respond (Stevense et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The reduced DIF responsiveness of the gefE− mutant is due to an increase in the threshold required to trigger a transcriptional response.
source: We, therefore, hypothesised that the reduced DIF responsiveness of the gefE− mutant was due to an increase in the threshold required to trigger a transcriptional response.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: GFP was expressed from the ecmA promoter in the same localization in slugs and fruiting bodies as has been previously described for ecmA-LacZ.
source: For this we replaced the endogenous copy of the ecmA gene with GFP (Figure 5A), and showed that GFP was expressed from the ecmA promoter in the same localization in slugs and fruiting bodies (Figure 5B) as has been previously described for ecmA-LacZ (Jermyn and Williams, 1991).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging shown in Figure 5B and comparison to cited literature.

claim: In wild type controls, increasing DIF concentrations resulted in greater numbers of GFP expressing cells, with only a small change in GFP expression level per cell.
source: As expected, in wild type controls, increasing DIF concentrations resulted in greater numbers of GFP expressing cells, with only a small change in GFP expression level per cell (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: At all concentrations of DIF, the number of responding gefE− mutant cells was lower than wild type.
source: Most importantly, at all concentrations of DIF, the number of responding gefE− mutant cells was lower than wild type (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: There was little difference in the level of ecmA:GFP expression between individual wild type or gefE− mutant responding cells.
source: However, there was little difference in the level of ecmA:GFP expression between individual wild type or gefE− mutant responding cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: gefE regulates the cell-intrinsic threshold at which cells respond to DIF.
source: Taken together, these data provide strong support for the idea that gefE regulates the cell-intrinsic threshold at which cells respond to DIF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FACS analysis of individual cell responses shown in Figure 5.

claim: gefE is predicted to encode a RasGEF.
source: As gefE is predicted to encode a RasGEF, whose primary function is to activate Ras proteins by catalyzing the exchange of GDP for GTP
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and known function of RasGEF domains.

claim: The Dictyostelium genome encodes 11 Ras proteins.
source: Although the Dictyostelium genome encodes 11 Ras proteins, only one, RasD, exhibits strong developmental expression (Reymond et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RasD exhibits strong developmental expression.
source: Although the Dictyostelium genome encodes 11 Ras proteins, only one, RasD, exhibits strong developmental expression (Reymond et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The level of both RasD expression and GTP bound activated RasD are significantly higher in cells grown in the absence of glucose.
source: Furthermore, we found that the level of both RasD expression and GTP bound activated RasD are significantly higher in cells grown in the absence of glucose (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GefE and RasD mutant cells have previously been shown to exhibit identical slug phototaxis defects.
source: Finally, GefE and RasD mutant cells have previously been shown to exhibit identical slug phototaxis defects (Wilkins et al., 2000, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In 12 hr developed cells, the level of activated RasD was significantly lower in gefE− mutant cells.
source: In 12 hr developed cells, the level of activated RasD was significantly lower in gefE− mutant cells, although there was no difference in the total level of the RasD protein (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was no difference in the total level of the RasD protein between wild type and gefE− mutant cells.
source: In 12 hr developed cells, the level of activated RasD was significantly lower in gefE− mutant cells, although there was no difference in the total level of the RasD protein (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was no corresponding decrease in the levels of activated RasG, RasB, RasC or Rap1 in gefE− mutant cells.
source: In addition, there was no corresponding decrease in the levels of activated RasG, RasB, RasC or Rap1 (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments not shown.

claim: GefE is the predominant activator of RasD and is specific for RasD.
source: These results suggest that GefE is the predominant activator of RasD and is specific for RasD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the specificity of RasD activation defects in gefE− mutant.

claim: When labelled wild type cells were mixed with rasD− mutant cells, the labelled cells accumulated in the pstO and pstB populations and were underrepresented in the prespore population.
source: When labelled wild type cells were mixed with rasD− mutant cells, the labelled cells accumulated in the pstO and pstB populations and were underrepresented in the prespore population (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of chimeric slugs shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When RasD expression levels were elevated in wild type cells or cells were forced to express constitutively active rasD(G12T), these cells exhibited a strong localization towards the pstB region at the rear of slug and in the lower cup of fruiting bodies when mixed with wild type cells.
source: Moreover, when RasD expression levels were elevated in wild type cells or cells were forced to express constitutively active rasD(G12T), these cells exhibited a strong localization towards the pstB region at the rear of slug and in the lower cup of fruiting bodies when mixed with wild type cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of chimeric development shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Unlike wild type cells, the effect of RasD overexpression on cell fate was only observed in gefE− mutant cells which expressed constitutively active rasD(G12T).
source: Importantly, unlike wild type cells, this effect was only observed in gefE− mutant cells which expressed constitutively active rasD(G12T).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the effects of RasD and RasD(G12T) overexpression in wild type vs gefE− mutant backgrounds shown in Figure 6D.

claim: RasD is normally converted to its GTP bound form upon activation by GefE.
source: These findings thus suggest that RasD is normally converted to its GTP bound form upon activation by GefE
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical and genetic data on GefE and RasD.

claim: GefE and RasD coordinate DIF dependent lineage bias.
source: and support the idea that GefE and RasD coordinate DIF dependent lineage bias.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the totality of experiments on GefE and RasD function.

claim: gefE was found to be uniformly expressed in all cells during growth.
source: For this, gefE or rasD promoter sequences were used to drive RFP expression. Although gefE was found to be uniformly expressed in all cells during growth, rasD expression was highly heterogeneous (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter gene expression shown in Figure 7A.

claim: rasD expression was highly heterogeneous during growth.
source: For this, gefE or rasD promoter sequences were used to drive RFP expression. Although gefE was found to be uniformly expressed in all cells during growth, rasD expression was highly heterogeneous (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter gene expression shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The rasD promoter RFP reporter construct shows strong developmental regulation and drives prestalk cell specific expression at the slug and culminant stages.
source: The rasD promoter RFP reporter construct used here shows strong developmental regulation and drives prestalk cell specific expression at the slug and culminant stages (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports using rasD:lacZ (Esch and Firtel, 1991; Jermyn and Williams, 1995) and observations of the endogenous transcripts (Maeda et al., 2003)
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Growth of cells in G− medium resulted in a significant increase in the number of rasD:RFP expressing cells.
source: Firstly, we found that growth of cells in G− medium (conditions that increase the likelihood of DIF dependent lineage choice) resulted in a significant increase in the number of rasD:RFP expressing cells (73 ± 3% to 89 ± 5%)
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from reporter gene expression analysis.

claim: No change in gefE:RFP expression was observed when cells were grown in G− medium.
source: whereas no change was observed in gefE:RFP expressing cells.
evidence: This is an observation from reporter gene expression analysis.

claim: Cells expressing lower levels of RasD were found to be less likely to differentiate as prestalk cells than prespore cells.
source: Secondly, growing rasD:RFP expressing cells were sorted by FACS based on their fluorescence and developed in chimera with wild type cells. Cells expressing lower levels of RasD were found to be less likely to differentiate as prestalk cells than prespore cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS sorting and chimeric development shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cells expressing high rasD transcript levels can form both prespore and prestalk cells.
source: Surprisingly, however, cells expressing high rasD transcript levels can form both prespore and prestalk cells, as evidenced by their random distribution at both slug and culminant stages (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of chimeric development shown in Figure 7B.

claim: rasD high or rasD low expressing cells quickly returned to pre-sorted equilibrium when purified by FACS and regrown in culture.
source: In order to test whether RasD behaves in this fashion, rasD high or rasD low expressing cells were purified by FACS and then regrown in culture. Each population quickly returned to its pre-sorted equilibrium (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis over time shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The low RasD expressing population exhibits slightly faster dynamics than the high RasD expressing population.
source: It is interesting to note, however, that the low RasD expressing population exhibits slightly faster dynamics than the high RasD expressing population
evidence: This is an observation from the dynamics data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Population heterogeneity is generated by dynamic rasD expression in vegetative cells.
source: Together these findings suggest that population heterogeneity is generated by dynamic rasD expression in vegetative cells
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reporter gene expression and dynamics experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Extrinsic factors such as nutritional history affect the position of the dynamic equilibrium of rasD expression.
source: and that extrinsic factors such as nutritional history affect the position of this dynamic equilibrium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that G− growth increases rasD expression.

claim: Transcription of rasD is heterogeneous in growing cells.
source: We find that transcription of rasD is heterogeneous in growing cells
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter gene expression shown in Figure 7A.

claim: RasD activity is controlled by a ubiquitously expressed RasGEF, gefE.
source: whilst its activity is controlled by a ubiquitously expressed RasGEF, gefE.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the uniform expression of gefE and its requirement for RasD activation.

claim: Expression of GefE is required to activate RasD in a subset of cells.
source: Expression of GefE is required to activate RasD in a subset of cells
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reduced RasD-GTP levels in gefE− mutant and heterogeneous rasD expression.

claim: RasD activation sets the threshold at which cells respond to the pstB/pstO differentiation inducer DIF.
source: which in turn sets the threshold at which these cells respond to the pstB/pstO differentiation inducer DIF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the DIF response threshold experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Initial studies carried out in cell lines expressing constitutively activated Ras(G12T) suggested Ras signaling played a key role in prestalk cell differentiation.
source: Initial studies carried out in cell lines expressing constitutively activated Ras(G12T) suggested Ras signaling played a key role in prestalk cell differentiation (Jaffer, 2000; Jaffer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Disruption of the gene encoding RasD was reported not to affect cell fate specification during clonal development.
source: However, disruption of the gene encoding RasD, the major developmentally expressed Ras protein, was reported not to affect cell fate specification during clonal development (Wilkins et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There was compensatory upregulation of the highly related RasG protein during development in both rasD− and gefE− mutant backgrounds.
source: We found that there was indeed compensatory upregulation of the highly related RasG protein during development in both rasD− and gefE− mutant backgrounds (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments not shown.

claim: Compensatory upregulation of RasG did not affect lineage bias in chimeras with wild type cells.
source: but that this did not affect lineage bias in chimeras with wild type cells.
evidence: This is an observation from chimeric development experiments.

claim: GefE-mediated activation of RasD is uniquely important to confer lineage bias in Dictyostelium.
source: This suggests that GefE-mediated activation of RasD is uniquely important to confer lineage bias in Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the specificity of GefE-RasD effects on lineage bias.

claim: Cells of the inner cell mass (ICM) adopt either primitive endoderm (PrE) or epiblast (EPI) fates in a position independent fashion.
source: For example, in one of the earliest lineage choices made during mouse embryogenesis, cells of the inner cell mass (ICM) adopt either primitive endoderm (PrE) or epiblast (EPI) fates. This occurs in a position independent fashion with ICM cells exhibiting seemingly stochastic expression of PrE and EPI markers (Dietrich and Hiiragi, 2007; Plusa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on mouse development.

claim: Heterogeneity in responsiveness to differentiation inducing signals, such as the PrE inducer FGF, underlies salt and pepper differentiation in the mouse ICM.
source: It has been proposed that heterogeneity in responsiveness to differentiation inducing signals, such as the PrE inducer FGF, underlies this salt and pepper differentiation (Yamanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on mouse development.

claim: Pattern formation based on stochastic salt and pepper differentiation and sorting out is likely to be a fundamental and deeply conserved developmental patterning mechanism.
source: Pattern formation based on stochastic salt and pepper differentiation and sorting out is likely to be a fundamental and deeply conserved developmental patterning mechanism (Kay and Thompson, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation and comparison across organisms.

claim: Initial cell fate choice and pattern formation in Dictyostelium discoideum is based on salt and pepper differentiation and sorting out.
source: One route to understanding this phenomenon comes from the finding that initial cell fate choice and pattern formation in Dictyostelium discoideum, a genetically and biochemically tractable organism with a small number of easily recognizable cell types, is based on this mechanism (Thompson et al., 2004b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Upon starvation, Dictyostelium cells enter a developmental cycle that begins with the aggregation of several thousand cells to make a multicellular mound.
source: Upon starvation, Dictyostelium cells enter a developmental cycle that begins with the aggregation of several thousand cells to make a multicellular mound.
evidence: This is a description of the Dictyostelium developmental cycle based on established knowledge.

claim: Within the mound, cells differentiate intermingled into prestalk or prespore cells.
source: Within the mound, cells differentiate intermingled into prestalk or prespore cells.
evidence: This is a description of Dictyostelium development based on established knowledge.

claim: After sorting out, the different cell types are organized into discrete tissues in the migratory slug.
source: After sorting out, the different cell types are organized into discrete tissues in the migratory slug.
evidence: This is a description of Dictyostelium development based on established knowledge.

claim: Prestalk cells occupy the anterior 25% of the slug.
source: Prestalk cells occupy the anterior 25% of the slug, with anterior like cells also found scattered within the prespore zone.
evidence: This is a description of Dictyostelium slug organization based on established knowledge.

claim: DIF is primarily required for pstB cell differentiation, with a more minor role in pstO cell differentiation.
source: Secondly, biases established during growth have been shown to affect the sensitivity of cells to differentiation signals experienced during development, such as the chlorinated alkyl phenone DIF-1 (hereafter termed DIF), which is primarily required for pstB cell differentiation, with a more minor role in pstO cell differentiation (Thompson and Kay, 2000b; Thompson et al., 2004a; Zhukovskaya et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2006b; Keller and Thompson, 2008; Saito et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: 'Stalky' biased cells are more sensitive to DIF in monolayer culture assays than 'sporey' biased cells.
source: For example, 'stalky' biased cells are more sensitive to DIF in monolayer culture assays than 'sporey' biased cells (Thompson and Kay, 2000a; Kubohara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Immediate-early gene responses to DIF exhibit all-or-none behavior, leading to population level heterogeneity.
source: Finally, immediate-early gene responses to DIF exhibit all-or-none behavior, leading to population level heterogeneity (Stevense et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Dictyostelium strains were cultured on lawns of Klebsiella aerogenes or in HL5 medium with (G+) or without (G−) 86 mM glucose.
